extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, law students and practitioners interested in defamation law
extracted.subtask_description: A broad, cross-jurisdictional explanatory overview of defamation (libel and slander) covering core legal elements, common defenses, terminology differences, modern issues (internet/cyber libel), and variations between jurisdictions. Useful as a reference for understanding what makes a statement actionable and how laws and protections interact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five essential elements to defamation
rubrics_metrics.description: There are five essential elements to defamation: (1) The accusation is false; and (2) it impeaches the subject's character; and (3) it is published to a third person; and (4) it damages the reputation of the subject; and (5) that the accusation is done intentionally or with fault such as wanton disregard of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formulation (quoted from a practitioner's guide) lists the classic elements plaintiffs must typically prove in a defamation action: falsity, defamatory meaning, publication, reputational harm, and fault/intent. Jurisdictions may vary in how fault is defined and in damages requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Libel vs slander (form-based distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Libel refers to written defamatory statements; slander refers to oral statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that libel 'encompasses communications occurring in "physical form"' and that defamatory statements on records and computer tapes are considered libel rather than slander. Different rules (e.g., presumptions about damages) historically applied to libel vs slander, though modern statutes may unify treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Falsity requirement / truth as a defence
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement can only be defamatory if it is false; therefore true statements of fact about others, regardless of the damage rendered, are not defamatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple sources cited reiterate truth as a central defense to defamation. Historical cases (e.g., John Peter Zenger) are noted in relation to truth as a defence, but the article warns the Zenger outcome involved jury nullification rather than legal acquittal. How courts treat truth can vary by jurisdiction and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication to a third person
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamatory conduct must be communicated to someone other than the plaintiff (published to a third person).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is one of the five essential elements; online comments and republications count as publication. Jurisdictions may differ about what counts as republication and who is liable for repeated or shared content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damage to reputation (harm/damages)
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement must damage the reputation of the subject (produce reputational harm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some doctrines (e.g., defamation per se) and statutes affect whether plaintiffs must plead or prove actual damages. Remedies and the quantum of damages vary widely across cases and jurisdictions (examples in the article cite large awards and compensatory schemes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fault/intent standard (including actual malice for public figures)
rubrics_metrics.description: The accusation must be done intentionally or with fault such as wanton disregard of facts; public officials/public figures may need to prove 'actual malice' (knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for truth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article references landmark U.S. law (New York Times Co. v. Sullivan) establishing the actual malice standard for some plaintiffs. Fault standards differ by jurisdiction, plaintiff status (private vs public), and statutory scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion vs fact / limits of opinion privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction between fact and opinion affects defamation liability, but 'a number of common law jurisdictions no longer recognize any legal distinction between fact and opinion' and the U.S. Supreme Court has held the First Amendment does not require an opinion privilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because opinions that imply false facts can be actionable, courts examine whether a statement is reasonably understood as asserting provable facts. Cases such as Milkovich are relevant to the line between protected opinion and actionable statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defences: fair comment / honest opinion and other privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognised defences and privileges include fair comment/fair criticism and other qualified or absolute privileges that may protect defamatory statements in certain contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites 'Opinion and Fair Comment Privileges' and similar doctrines; their availability and scope vary by jurisdiction (e.g., statutory reforms, protections for political speech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional terminology differences (tort vs delict) and comparative law
rubrics_metrics.description: Different legal systems use different terminology and conceptual frameworks (e.g., 'tort' vs 'delict'); the article explains that 'delict' is used in some civil and mixed jurisdictions while 'tort' is the general term in comparative law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology affects how rules are described and where to find statutes/case law. The article gives examples (Scots law, South African law, Civil Code of PRC using 'tortfeasor').

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal defamation and decriminalisation trends
rubrics_metrics.description: Some countries criminalise defamation; others have moved to decriminalise it. The article notes maps and country-specific penal codes that criminalise defamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece references international reports and national statutes showing wide variation—criminal penalties exist in many jurisdictions and international bodies have called for decriminalisation or caution in criminalising speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet / cyber libel (online publication constitutes libel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet publications such as defamatory comments on social media can also constitute libel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights modern issues: online republication, jurisdictional reach of online postings, liability for platforms, and specific 'cyber libel' statutes or prosecutions in some countries. Cases and statutes (e.g., Duffy v Google Inc., national cybercrime laws) illustrate evolving doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation of corporations and group libel
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation can affect corporate entities and groups; doctrines and remedies for corporate reputation and 'group libel' are recognised and have specific analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites sources on corporate defamation and academic work on group libel; some jurisdictions limit claims by very large or indistinct groups, while corporations may bring claims subject to particular rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic lawsuits against public participation (SLAPP) and libel tourism
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural and policy concerns such as SLAPP suits (lawsuits intended to silence critics) and 'libel tourism' (filing suits in favorable jurisdictions) are identified as significant issues surrounding defamation law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article references anti‑SLAPP statutes (e.g., California CCP §425.16, Ontario's Protection of Public Participation Act) and international critiques; these doctrines affect access to remedies and free-expression balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of freedom of expression protections in developing defamation case law
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutions and human-rights instruments (e.g., Section 2 of the Canadian Charter, the U.S. First Amendment) require courts to take freedom of expression into account when developing defamation law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that free-speech protections shape doctrines like actual malice, public-interest defenses, and statutory reform—courts balance reputation interests against expression rights differently across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and comparative variation in doctrines and statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation law has evolved historically and varies by jurisdiction; examples and case law from many countries show different statutory frameworks, reforms, and judicial approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article compiles many national statutes, case citations, and international reports (OSCE, UNESCO, Article 19) to show the breadth of doctrinal variation. Practitioners must consult local law for precise standards.
